extracted.intended_audience: machine-learning researchers and practitioners studying LLM mathematical reasoning, robustness, and dataset/benchmark design
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, curating, and evaluating a benchmark (MATH-Perturb) to measure large language models' robustness to simple and hard perturbations of hard math problems. Includes annotation rubrics, evaluation protocols, metrics, and failure-mode analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the Dataset (seed selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use level-5 (hardest) problems from the MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021) as the seed problems. Use level-5 problems from both the train split and the test split as seeds so behavior on both splits can be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on hardest problems because state-of-the-art models already achieve high accuracy on easier levels. Problems may contain LaTeX/Asymptote graphics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation Criterion — MATH-P-Simple (simple perturbation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a modified problem as a simple perturbation: make non-essential modifications such that the modified problem can be solved using the same method as the original problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: numerical modifications, asking for a different but related quantity, adding/removing non-essential constraints, changing a mathematical concept to its contrasting counterpart. Ensure the reasoning pattern remains the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation Criterion — MATH-P-Hard (hard perturbation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a modified problem as a hard perturbation: apply small but fundamental modifications so the modified problem cannot be solved using the same method as the original and requires deeper math understanding and harder problem-solving skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General strategies: increase the complexity of mathematical objects (e.g., raise polynomial degree), alter key numbers to make brute-force infeasible, relax constraints to cover more general cases, change essential conditions so original simplifying properties (symmetry, reducibility, linearity) no longer hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal Edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators must make as minimal modifications as possible to the original problem text so the modified problems stay close in text form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tests generalization and elicits memorization behaviors; minimal edits keep lexical similarity high even when problem formula changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changed Answers
rubrics_metrics.description: For both simple and hard modifications, guarantee that the answers to the modified problems are different from the original answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents models from 'cheating' by pattern recognition or outputting memorized original answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Control — annotator qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit annotators with strong mathematical backgrounds: annotators were PhD students with bachelor’s degrees in mathematics, research experience in theoretical ML, and/or mathematical competition experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert annotators to ensure correctness and appropriate difficulty changes when perturbing hard-level problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Control — annotation workflow (double-check and cross-validation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require annotators to double-check their annotations; each modified problem is cross-validated by an independent annotator to ensure the answer is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually review problematic cases (e.g., where a model's answer differs from the annotated answer) and remove annotations failing quality checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual verification for model-disagreement cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Manually inspect and confirm annotated answers for problems where a model (o1-mini in this study) and the annotator disagree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures benchmark answers are reliable even when models produce alternative outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity quantification between original and perturbed problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify similarity using (1) normalized edit distance (edit distance normalized by original problem length) and (2) cosine similarity between embeddings of the two problems using OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report distributions of normalized edit distances and cosine similarities to show lexical/semantic closeness; useful to characterize how 'minimal' edits are and to interpret model behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval-based similarity metric (MRR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) when using the perturbed problem as a query to retrieve the corresponding original problem from the full set of original problems using cosine similarity of embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High MRR (close to 1) indicates the perturbed problem retrieves its original counterpart, showing closeness under typical semantic retrieval methods (reported: 0.995 for MATH-P-Simple, 0.986 for MATH-P-Hard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation strategy taxonomy — simple perturbation examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate common strategies for simple perturbations: numerical modifications; asking for a different but related quantity; adding/removing non-essential constraints; other non-essential lexical or numeric changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators verify that these modifications do not alter the fundamental reasoning pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation strategy taxonomy — hard perturbation examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate common strategies for hard perturbations: increasing complexity of mathematical objects; altering key numbers to disable brute-force methods; relaxing constraints to generalize cases; modifying essential conditions so simplifying properties no longer hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These changes aim to force different solving methods and deeper theorems rather than computational shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation protocol — zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting as the standard evaluation method for model responses on the benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to elicit reasoning steps; referenced works include Wei et al. (2022) and Kojima et al. (2022).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool usage prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Disallow any tool usage during evaluation, including access to code interpreters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precludes trivial brute-force programmatic solutions that would defeat the intent of testing reasoning robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer equivalence checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether a generated answer matches the ground-truth answer by first performing string normalization and then using the sympy package to check equivalence of two mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows precedent from Hendrycks et al. (2021) and Shao et al. (2024); necessary to accept mathematically equivalent expressions that differ lexically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmark a wide range of models, including long-CoT models, closed-source large models, open-sourced smaller models, and math-specific models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and report version information; diversity helps understand how robustness varies across model classes and sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary reported metric — accuracy (%) across variants and splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Report model accuracy (%) on Original problems, MATH-P-Simple, and MATH-P-Hard; also report accuracies separately for problems originating from train and test splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these comparisons to quantify performance drops due to perturbations and possible data-contamination/generalization effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error rate reporting and visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Report error rates (%) for Original, Simple (0-shot), Simple (ICL), Hard (0-shot), Hard (ICL) and visualize differences to show ICL and perturbation impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose error-rate changes into components attributable to ICL gains and misleading effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure-mode categorization (Case I–IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify each triple (Original, Simple, Hard) response correctness into four cases: Case I — at least one of Original/Simple correct and Hard correct; Case II — Original and Simple incorrect and Hard incorrect; Case III — Original and Simple incorrect but Hard correct; Case IV — at least one of Original/Simple correct but Hard incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute percentages of responses in each case per model to characterize generalization/failure patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative failure-mode taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify common error types when models face harder problems: mistakes in basic numerical computations and algebra, unjustified claims, missed cases, and lack of specific math knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are considered general failure modes more prominent in weaker models; stronger models show fewer such basic errors and more memorization-related failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorization detection and characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect forms of memorization beyond verbatim recitation: (a) models ignore modified assumptions and assume original assumptions hold; (b) models blindly apply learned problem-solving techniques without judging applicability; (c) models may output desired outcomes from original problems rather than the modified target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify via manual inspection and via nsame (number of errors where final answer equals original-answer); compute normalized edit distances between responses to identify superficial vs semantic collapse. Estimate proportion of errors due to memorization per model (e.g., 40% for o1-mini, 25% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet in manual samples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode collapse measurement (nsame and edit distances)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each model, report nsame: number of problems where the model’s final answer equals the corresponding original problem's ground-truth; also compute normalized edit distance between full response to modified problem and response to original problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these statistics to determine whether errors are due to naive recitation (mode collapse) or more subtle ignoring of changed assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-context learning (ICL) evaluation and decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate one-shot ICL using the corresponding original (problem, solution) as demonstration. Decompose ICL influence on MATH-P-Hard into: n_wrong→correct (ICL effect that reduces errors) and n_correct→wrong (misleading effect that increases errors); normalize percentages appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large models often show both ICL gains and substantial misleading effects; net improvements on MATH-P-Hard are marginal for most models.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICL ablation — original vs random example
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare one-shot ICL using the corresponding original example versus using a random example from the same category to assess specificity of the demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICL with the original problem and solution typically outperforms ICL with a random example; report the exception cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference-time scaling metrics (pass@k and self-consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure inference-time scaling by computing pass@k (generate N independent solutions and compute pass@k formula) and self-consistency (majority-vote among k sampled responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose N (e.g., N=64 for some models, N=8 for others) and report pass@k and self-consistency accuracies with standard deviation. Use to study gains from increased inference compute and sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting dataset statistics and subject distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Report final dataset size (279 pairs after quality-control removals), counts from train/test splits (164 train, 115 test), and distribution across subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting & Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, Precalculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide per-subject counts and percentages to contextualize difficulty distribution across mathematical topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-tool/no-brute-force rule justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Disallow tool access explicitly because many perturbed problems could be solved trivially by brute-force programmatic search, which would not test reasoning robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the evaluation protocol; enforce across all model evaluations.
